findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: 2025/26 service expenditure delivered £1.624 million under budget
findings.detail: The Council's net expenditure on services for 2025/26 was £1.624 million under the approved budget. This underspend was transferred to reserves, increasing the opening cash balance and contributing to higher-than-forecast cash availability in 2026/27. The budget for 2026/27 opening cash was set at £40 million, but actual was £41.9 million.
findings.matters: Consistent underspends raise questions about budget accuracy and whether planned services are being delivered at anticipated levels. Combined with capital slippage, it suggests the council may not be deploying budgeted expenditure as planned.
findings.figures: £1.624 million underspend, £41.9 million opening balance vs £40.0 million budgeted
findings.quote: The Council's net expenditure on services for 2025/26 was £1.624 million under budget and this was transferred to reserves, increasing the opening cash balance as at 1 April 2026.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Investment income of £2.2 million flagged as an important source of revenue budget funding, but forecast interest rates are falling
findings.detail: The Council's treasury advisors (MUFG) forecast interest rates will fall from 3.75% now to 3.50% in Q2 2027 and further to 3.25% by end of March 2028. The council is currently forecasting £2.2 million in investment interest for 2026/27, and the finance team explicitly note this is 'an important source of income for the Council's revenue budget'. As rates fall, this income will compress.
findings.matters: If investment income is essential to the revenue budget, a 0.25% rate cut reduces annual income by approximately £130,000 on the current £53.3 million portfolio. Budgets that rely on interest windfalls become unstable as policy rates fall.
findings.figures: £2,200,000 forecast, average rate 4.13%, base rate forecast to fall to 3.50%, then 3.25% by March 2028
findings.quote: The net investment interest is an important source of income for the Council's revenue budget.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: £14.074 million of capital projects rescheduled from 2025/26 into 2026/27
findings.detail: Capital projects totalling £14.074 million planned for 2025/26 were rescheduled into the current financial year. This is a primary reason why the opening cash balance was £41.9 million instead of the £40.0 million budgeted. The slippage means capital was not deployed at the pace expected last year.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippage indicates the council has not delivered capital projects on schedule, raising questions about procurement, planning, or execution capacity that affect the reliability of future capital delivery.
findings.figures: £14.074 million
findings.quote: Capital projects totalling £14.074 million were rescheduled during 2025/26 into the 2026/27 financial year.

findings.headline: Grant Volatility reserve completely depleted (£2.001m drawn down to zero)
findings.detail: The Grant Volatility earmarked reserve, which typically exists to buffer fluctuations in government grant funding, has been completely drawn down with £2.001m in payments and no receipts. This reserve now stands at £0k.
findings.matters: Elimination of the grant volatility buffer leaves the council exposed to any unexpected reductions or delays in government funding streams, particularly significant during the unitary transition period when funding may be uncertain.

findings.headline: Capital and Revenue Initiatives reserve being depleted from £6.94m to £1.44m with £9.702m in payments
findings.detail: The largest earmarked reserve (Capital and Revenue Initiatives) shows payments of £9.702m against an opening balance of £6.94m, with receipts of only £4.201m. Combined with other reserve drawdowns, this leaves just £1.439m remaining from what was a substantial reserve.
findings.matters: Rapid depletion of earmarked reserves for capital and revenue initiatives suggests either one-off projects consuming accumulated funds, or underlying pressures requiring ongoing use of reserves rather than base budgets.
findings.figures: Opening balance £6,940k, payments £9,702k, receipts £4,201k, closing balance £1,439k

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Council is using internal borrowing (£3.687m) to fund capital projects not yet financed
findings.detail: The forecast notes £3.687m of internal borrowing 'still to be repaid' from projects not yet financed or from Minimum Revenue Provision. This indicates the council has drawn on its own reserves to fund capital expenditure, rather than securing external funding or managing within normal budget constraints.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing signals capital funding constraints and indicates the council is using reserves as a de facto lender; this reduces financial flexibility for dealing with emerging pressures or the unitary transition.

findings.quote: Internal Borrowing still to be repaid (projects not yet financed/MRP) (3,687)

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Usable reserves forecast to leave only £1.15m net position when transitioning to unitary authority in April 2028
findings.detail: Starting from £13.637m in usable reserves at 31/03/27, the council must commit £4.377m to 2027/28 projects, £1.984m to disability facilities grants that cannot be spent by the council, repay £3.687m of internal borrowing, and commit £2.439m to post-April 2028 projects. This sequence leaves only £1.15m to hand to the unitary authority.
findings.matters: Lenders assess reserve adequacy as key to financial resilience; a precipitous decline from £13.6m to £1.15m in 18 months suggests the council is consuming accumulated reserves rather than operating sustainably, and leaves minimal buffer for the transition.

findings.headline: Royal Victoria Place redevelopment risk escalated due to listed building status application causing timeline and cost impacts
findings.detail: The council's risk assessment for the Royal Victoria Place (RVP) redevelopment has been increased following an application for listed building status affecting 5-7 Camden Road. The council submitted a Certificate of Immunity from Listing (COIL) to Historic England with outcome expected mid-August/early September 2026. The decision will enable the council to plan the programme and identify how to mitigate for lost time. Additional uncertainty exists as local government reorganisation could result in a shadow authority making future decisions about RVP rather than Tunbridge Wells Borough Council.
findings.matters: A lender financing a council's capital schemes needs visibility on project delays and cost escalation risk, particularly when dependent on heritage exemptions and when governance uncertainty could pass decisions to a successor authority.

findings.quote: Due to the impact on the development timeline and costs brought about by an application for listed building status of 5-7 Camden Road, the risk for the re-development of Royal Victora Place (RVP) had been increased.

findings.headline: Usable reserves forecast to decline from £23,421k to just £3,000k by 2029/30
findings.detail: The council's total usable reserves of £23,421k at 31 March 2026 will be heavily committed, with £17,175k already earmarked for capital and revenue projects from 2026/27 onwards and £3,246k in outstanding financing. This leaves only £3,000k in forecast usable reserves by 2029/30—an 87% reduction over four years.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial resilience through reserve levels; a steep decline from £23m to £3m (just 3-4% of typical council budget) signals tightening financial flexibility and reduced capacity to absorb unexpected demand, service pressures, or borrowing costs.

findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether capital deferrals reflect delivery barriers, cost escalation, resource constraints, or planning challenges. Material deferrals of this scale suggest the council may not be able to complete its capital programme as planned.

findings.headline: Council is currently debt-free but retains borrowing flexibility for schemes with positive financial returns
findings.detail: Financial principles confirm the council carries no external debt and will only borrow where 'a scheme is able to cover its funding costs'. This maintains flexibility but also means no immediate borrowing headroom is committed to close the identified deficits.
findings.matters: Debt-free status is positive but does not reduce the urgency of closing the structural deficit. It does confirm borrowing capacity exists if needed, but also suggests the council has not yet committed to use borrowing to fund the savings gap.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F Savings and Efficiency Plan 2026-28
findings.headline: Council acquired Royal Victoria Place shopping centre in 2023, representing major leverage of reserve position
findings.detail: Cabinet member notes the council purchased Royal Victoria Place shopping centre in 2023 and explicitly states it 'would never have been able to do this without maintaining a strong reserve position.' This is a significant asset acquisition on the balance sheet and represents a strategic investment decision.
findings.matters: A lender assesses covenant quality partly on reserve adequacy and partly on capital deployment discipline. A retail property acquisition during a period of identified structural budget deficits warrants scrutiny on expected returns and financial discipline.
findings.figures: Shopping centre purchase 2023.
findings.quote: An example of this was the ability of the Council to purchase the Royal Victoria Place shopping centre in 2023. We would never have been able to do this without maintaining a strong reserve position.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F Savings and Efficiency Plan 2026-28
findings.headline: Council drew £2.1m from reserves in 2026/27 to balance budget, then faces multi-year deficits
findings.detail: The savings table shows a £2.1m reserve draw in 2026/27 to balance that year's budget (bringing total funding to equal net budget), then zero reserve use thereafter as deficits appear. This is a one-off cushion that is now consumed.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns to balance operational budgets indicate the underlying position is already in deficit and become unsustainable if repeated. The absence of further draws in the forecast suggests the plan assumes significant savings delivery or revenue growth that is not yet committed.
findings.figures: Reserves funding 2026/27: £2,100k; 2027/28 onwards: £0k.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F Savings and Efficiency Plan 2026-28
findings.headline: Council holds £147m asset base and is executing disposal strategy to fund reserves and capital
findings.detail: The council states it owns around £147m of long-term assets. Strategy is to dispose of surplus assets via Property Asset Oversight Panel to 'resume capital receipts to fund the capital programme' and restore reserves to pre-pandemic levels (targeting £4m minimum). This indicates reliance on asset sales for financial sustainability.
findings.matters: Asset disposal is a one-off revenue source that cannot be sustained. A lender needs to understand the scale of sales planned and whether the council can reach a structurally balanced position without ongoing disposals.
findings.figures: £147m of long-term assets; £4m minimum reserve target; proceeds of capital disposals to be prioritised to restore reserves.
findings.quote: The Council owns around £147m worth of long-term assets, maintaining them at a considerable cost. We need to look at disposing of any that are no longer showing good value for the taxpayer.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F Savings and Efficiency Plan 2026-28
findings.headline: External auditor flagged budget gaps in 2025 VFM conclusion, recommending immediate savings plan development
findings.detail: The 2025 Annual Report included a specific improvement recommendation that the council develop a council-wide savings programme to address 'significant budget gaps identified from 2027/28'. This document is the formal response to that audit finding.
findings.matters: An audit recommendation about budget sustainability is a material governance finding that signals the external auditor had concerns about forward financial planning. It indicates the audit risk assessment and may affect the council's CIPFA financial resilience rating.
findings.figures: External Auditor Annual Report year ending 31 March 2025.
findings.quote: The External Auditor's Annual Report for the year ending 31 March 2025 made an improvement recommendation in their Value for Money Conclusion that: The Council should develop a Council-wide savings and efficiency programme in order to address the significant budget gaps identified from 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F Savings and Efficiency Plan 2026-28
findings.headline: Major service contracts renewing at materially higher costs with limited cost mitigation identified
findings.detail: Waste & Street Cleansing and Leisure Centre management contracts are up for renewal with the council explicitly stating costs 'will be far higher this time around' due to market changes. These represent significant annual commitments but the plan identifies only £250k annual savings from waste vehicle capex and no specific mitigation for leisure costs.
findings.matters: Contract escalation is a direct hit to operating costs and a key driver of the medium-term deficit. A lender needs to understand whether these cost increases are manageable within council tax and retained business rates revenue.
findings.figures: £250k annual potential savings from waste vehicle capex (2027/28 onwards); contracts identified as renewing at 'significantly higher costs'.
findings.quote: The need for further savings is necessary as our major external contracts covering Waste & Street Cleansing and the management of our Leisure Centres are all up for renewal and the costs will be far higher this time around.

findings.headline: Leisure income removed entirely: £290k cut from 2027/28
findings.detail: The budget assumptions show leisure income will remain frozen and then £290k will be removed from 2027/28 onwards. This is a planned income loss, not a growth assumption, which adds to the deficit pressure.
findings.matters: A planned £290k removal of leisure income suggests a service change, asset disposal, or withdrawal from a commercial activity. This signals shifting council priorities and reduces the income base available to cover core services.
findings.quote: Leisure income remains frozen then £290k of income is removed from 2027/28

findings.headline: Waste and street cleansing costs rise 6% annually plus a step change of £5.3m from 2027/28
findings.detail: Beyond 6% annual increases, the budget assumptions include a material step change of £5.3m for waste and street cleansing from 2027/28 onwards. This represents either a new contractual commitment, service expansion, or significant price shock in this service area.
findings.matters: A £5.3m step change in a single service signals a major cost driver that may indicate contract renewal pressures or demand increases in waste management. Understanding this is essential for assessing cost control and sustainability.
findings.figures: £5.3m from 2027/28; 6% annual growth
findings.quote: Waste & Street Cleansing costs increase by 6% each year plus £5.3m from 2027/28

findings.headline: Unmanaged cumulative deficit totals £31.3 million over five years
findings.detail: The medium-term budget projections show that if left unmanaged, the five-year deficits would accumulate to £31,301k. This is the total fiscal gap that the council must address through savings, service changes, or other interventions.
findings.matters: A £31m cumulative deficit signals material structural fiscal stress. Lenders will require evidence of a credible savings plan to close this gap; without one, the council faces declining reserves and increased borrowing pressure.
findings.figures: £31,301k cumulative; £31.3 million
findings.quote: 31,301 IF LEFT UNMANAGEDNET MEDIUM-TERM CUMULATIVE FORECAST

findings.headline: Structural deficit: demand pressures are growing faster than the 3% income cap in years 2–5
findings.detail: Deficits of £4,893k (2028/29), £6,127k (2029/30), £7,373k (2030/31), and £8,452k (2031/32) are all attributed to 'Demand pressures greater than income cap of 3 per cent'. This escalating pattern shows demand is outpacing capped income growth and creating a structural fiscal mismatch.
findings.matters: A structural deficit where demand outpaces income growth signals the council must cut services, find efficiency savings, or accept successive years of larger shortfalls. This is a core lending risk and requires a credible savings plan.
findings.quote: Demand pressures greater than income cap of 3 per cent

findings.headline: Contract reprocurement adds a sharp £4.5m deficit in 2027/28
findings.detail: A single-year cost of £4,456k is identified for 2027/28 driven by 'market cost of reprocuring major contracts'. This is a specific, quantified pressure distinct from ongoing demand growth in subsequent years.
findings.matters: A £4.5m cost spike from contract reprocurement in a single year signals significant procurement or service commitments that will strain the budget in that year and need to be factored into financial planning.
findings.figures: £4,456k; £4.5 million
findings.quote: Market cost of reprocuring major contracts

findings.headline: Debt-free council may need to commence borrowing as reserves become 'largely allocated'
findings.detail: The council is currently debt-free with no external borrowing. However, the budget documentation notes that 'with reserves largely allocated, it may be necessary to commence borrowing to fund additional capital schemes'. The council maintains minimum reserve requirements of £3m (general reserves) and £1m (capital receipts), but has £2.1m transferred to earmarked reserves and £2,083,930 in new capital schemes pending approval.
findings.matters: A shift from debt-free status to external borrowing represents a material change in leverage and financial structure; this signals reserves are fully deployed and reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Current external debt: £0; minimum general reserves required: £3m; new capital schemes: £2,083,930
findings.quote: The Council has no external debt but, with reserves largely allocated, it may be necessary to commence borrowing to fund additional capital schemes. The Council does have the potential for using new capital receipts, building up usable reserves and access to internal and external borrowing.

findings.headline: Council has the lowest Core Spending Power in Kent, at £146 per capita
findings.detail: Tunbridge Wells has the lowest CSP (per-capita spending power from government and retained business rates) in Kent at £146 per capita. This structural underfunding versus peer councils limits service capacity and financial flexibility. The council notes it ranks only 219th out of 295 districts in deprivation, yet receives the least funding in its county.
findings.matters: Structural underfunding versus peer councils indicates the council has less financial resilience than comparators, limiting room to absorb pressures and suggesting lenders would perceive higher risk relative to better-funded peers.
findings.figures: TWBC CSP: £146 per capita (2026/27); CSP per 2025/26: £142 per capita; deprivation ranking 219 of 295; lowest in Kent
findings.quote: using the Government's own calculation TWBC has the lowest CSP in Kent at just £146 per capita (£142 in 2025/26 restated)

findings.headline: External auditor made formal improvement recommendation to develop council-wide savings programme
findings.detail: The external auditor's Value for Money Conclusion on the 2024/25 accounts included a formal recommendation that the council develop a council-wide savings and efficiency programme to address budget gaps from 2027/28. Only £405k in savings has been identified in the 2026/27 budget, despite council officers stating that 'the scope for further savings has been exhausted based on current policies and levels of service delivery'.
findings.matters: A formal audit recommendation suggests auditor concerns about financial sustainability; the gap between audit expectations and the council's stated savings capacity (£405k vs multimillion-pound deficits) indicates potential delivery risk.
findings.figures: Savings identified in 2026/27: £405k; budget gaps to address from 2027/28: £4.5m-£8.5m
findings.quote: The External Auditor Annual Report for the year ending 31 March 2025 made an improvement recommendation in their Value for Money Conclusion that: The Council should develop a Council-wide savings and efficiency programme in order to address the significant budget gaps identified from 2027/28.

findings.headline: Medium-term budget deficit growing from zero to £8.5 million over five years
findings.detail: While the 2026/27 budget is balanced, the council forecasts a structural deficit emerging and growing: £4.5m in 2027/28, £4.9m in 2028/29, £6.1m in 2029/30, £7.4m in 2030/31, and £8.5m in 2031/32. The council transferred £2.1m into earmarked reserves in 2026/27, but this provides only partial cushion against these projected deficits.
findings.matters: A consistent and growing structural deficit indicates the council cannot sustain its current service model; this creates material financial sustainability risk and suggests reserves will be drawn down or services must be cut significantly.
findings.quote: The significant increase to the budget gap in 2027/28 is due to the expiry of the waste and street sweeping contract on 31 March 2027, which is expected to more than double in cost from its current annual cost of £4.6million. The procurement of a new contract will be the largest service contract this council has ever awarded and is a major project requiring professional advice and resources from across the Council.

findings.headline: All three major service contracts expiring within 15 months with high risk of substantial cost increases
findings.detail: The council faces simultaneous renewal of three critical contracts: grounds maintenance (December 2026), waste and street sweeping (March 2027), and leisure centre management (March 2027). All were procured in a different economic climate. The council explicitly states that contractors now present significant cost increase risks due to pandemic impacts, rising National Living Wage and Employers' National Insurance increases, and loss of competitive market conditions.
findings.matters: Multiple critical service procurements in a compressed timeframe, in a weakened competitive environment, creates compounded procurement and delivery risk; failure across any of these contracts would force severe budget management.
findings.figures: Three contracts expiring: Dec 2026, March 2027, March 2027; waste contract alone currently £4.6m
findings.quote: The Council currently has in place three major contracts which were all procured in a very different economic climate and with the contractors being responsible for risks which have now come to pass. They were procured in a healthy and competitive marketplace which may now not be the case following the legacy of the pandemic and increases to the National Living Wage and Employers' National Insurance rates. This presents a significant risk to the Council in financial terms from potentially being exposed to additional risk going forwards.

findings.headline: Waste and street sweeping contract expected to more than double in cost from March 2027
findings.detail: The council's household waste collection and street cleaning contract expires 31 March 2027 with costs expected to double from the current £4.6 million annually. This single contract renewal is explicitly identified as the primary driver of the £4.5 million budget gap forecast for 2027/28. The council describes this as 'the largest service contract this council has ever awarded', signalling the scale of the procurement challenge.
findings.matters: A critical service contract doubling in cost creates material budget risk; cost overruns or procurement failure on this contract alone could force substantial service cuts or reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Current contract cost: £4.6m annually; expected to more than double; budget gap driven by this: £4.5m in 2027/28
findings.quote: The significant increase to the budget gap in 2027/28 is due to the expiry of the waste and street sweeping contract on 31 March 2027, which is expected to more than double in cost from its current annual cost of £4.6million.

findings.headline: Council holding ~£10 million in constrained Section 106 monies that limit overall cash flexibility
findings.detail: The council is holding approximately £10 million of unspent Section 106 contributions which are earmarked for specific purposes and cannot be freely deployed. It is also holding government-funded monies for the Local Authority Housing Fund and Homes for Ukraine scheme pending project expenditure.
findings.matters: These restricted funds reduce the council's operational liquidity and financial flexibility despite appearing on the balance sheet. Lenders need to understand that a significant portion of cash balances are committed to specific schemes.
findings.figures: ~£10 million in unspent Section 106 monies
findings.quote: The Council is currently holding in the region of £10 million of unspent Section 106 monies.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Treasury Management Policy & Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Investment income budget for 2026/27 expected at £2 million, down from £2.6 million in 2025/26 despite higher average investment balance
findings.detail: The council benefited from higher interest rates in 2025/26, earning £2.6 million on average funds of £56 million at 4.64%. For 2026/27, the interest budget is set at £2 million on average funds of £50.8 million at 3.94%, reflecting forecast falls in interest rates. The council notes it has locked in some longer-term investments at peak rates to mitigate this.
findings.matters: The decline in investment income reflects both lower interest rate forecasts and reduced cash balances available to invest. This reduces a material revenue funding source and highlights the council's exposure to interest rate movements.
findings.figures: 2025/26: £2.6 million on £56 million at 4.64%; 2026/27: £2 million budgeted on £50.8 million at 3.94%

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Treasury Management Policy & Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Council currently under-borrowed but has £4.293 million of approved borrowing not yet drawn, managing it through internal cash instead
findings.detail: Tunbridge Wells has no external borrowing and is intentionally maintaining an under-borrowed position by using surplus cash and reserves to fund capital needs instead of borrowing. However, £4.293 million of projects have been approved for borrowing but remain unfunded through internal borrowing. This strategy is justified by expectations that medium and longer-dated borrowing rates will fall once inflation concerns abate.
findings.matters: The decision to remain under-borrowed while rates are elevated represents a deliberate timing strategy, but leaves approved capital projects unfunded. This matters to lenders assessing the council's actual debt trajectory and cash management discipline.
findings.figures: £4.293 million approved borrowing not yet drawn
findings.quote: There is approval for £4.293 million of projects in the capital programme to be funded through borrowing but to date this has been managed through internal borrowing using surplus working capital.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Treasury Management Policy & Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Usable reserves and investment balances declining sharply towards 2028/29, falling to near-zero reserves
findings.detail: The council's usable reserves are forecast to fall from £16.008 million in 2025/26 to £9.347 million by 2028/29. Reserve balances specifically drop from £5.112 million to zero by 2028/29. Investment balances fall from £37.262 million to £20.168 million over the same period, with most of the decline occurring after 2026/27.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce financial flexibility and resilience. The trajectory to zero reserve balances by 2028/29 is material and coincides with the RVP borrowing period, tightening the council's financial position significantly.
findings.quote: Reserve balances 5,112 2,901 0 [showing forecast decline to zero by 2028/29]

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Treasury Management Policy & Strategy 202627
findings.headline: Royal Victoria Place shopping centre redevelopment will require up to £68 million in external borrowing from 2027/28
findings.detail: In July 2025 Full Council approved progression of design for new shopping and leisure facilities plus adjacent homes at RVP. The feasibility report identified indicative costs up to £68 million depending on options taken. The treasury strategy assumes this will be funded from external borrowing, increasing the Operational Boundary from £25 million to £93 million from 2027/28 onwards.
findings.matters: This is a material increase in the council's debt profile that will significantly change its treasury risk and borrowing costs. Lenders need to understand this commitment and its funding implications.
findings.figures: Indicative costs up to £68 million; Operational Boundary increasing to £93 million from 2027/28 (currently £25 million)
findings.quote: In July 2025 Full Council agreed to progress with the design of new shopping and leisure facilities, along with adjacent new homes, at the Royal Victoria Place Shopping Centre. The feasibility report identified indicative costs of up to £68 million, depending on the options taken.

findings.headline: Climate investment needs constrained by limited central government funding and council tax cap
findings.detail: The council has committed to carbon neutrality by 2030 but states its 'ability to finance this has become severely limited due to insufficient funding from Central Government, inflationary pressures and the cap on Council Tax increases.' This creates competing priorities: climate investment vs. managing waste contract shock.
findings.matters: Unfunded mandates to deliver climate outcomes, combined with the waste contract cost shock, will force difficult prioritization decisions that could affect service quality or require higher external borrowing.
findings.figures: No quantified budget for climate investments disclosed in this document

findings.headline: Affordable housing completions have fallen sharply—from ~280 units in 2020-21 to ~70-80 in 2024-25—limiting the council's ability to house homeless applicants from the Housing Register
findings.detail: Affordable housing delivery declined significantly from 2020-21 and remains much lower than pre-pandemic levels. The paper attributes this to high inflation, rising borrowing and material costs, labour shortages, and Registered Providers' need to spend on existing stock to meet energy efficiency and regulatory standards rather than building new homes. This directly constrains the council's relief pathway: only 31.7% of relief cases are housed in Registered Provider tenancies.
findings.matters: Lack of affordable supply forces reliance on more expensive temporary accommodation or private rented sector solutions, directly raising service costs. It also limits social housing allocation to homeless households (only 10% of lettings reserved for Band D homelessness cases).

findings.paper_title: Appx C - TWHomelessness Strategic Review Apr25
findings.headline: The Renters Rights Bill is expected to spike demand for prevention services and strain the council's ability to access private rented sector solutions
findings.detail: The paper flags that abolition of Section 21 'no-fault' evictions will likely cause a spike in homelessness applications as the sector adjusts. The council already faces an affordability gap: market rents average £1,385/month against Local Housing Allowance of £797-£1,820 depending on bedroom size (16-24% gap). The Bill may make accessing private rented accommodation even harder, and the council will need to reconsider how to work with landlords.
findings.matters: Expected legislative change will increase service demand and erode the cost-control lever (private rented prevention) that has worked well to date. Finance directors need to model budget impact and landlords should expect higher homelessness-driven demand and pressure on housing supply.
findings.figures: Market rent £1,385/month; LHA ranges £797-£1,820; affordability gaps range 16-24%
findings.quote: The Renters Right Bill is a significant proposed law introduced into Parliament and currently progressing through Parliament and expected to receive Royal Assent later in 2025... With the Renters Right Bill looming, there is likely to be an impact of this new legislation over the next few years as the sector adjusts to this. There is likely to be a spike in the number of households seeking housing assistance for this cause, until the abolition of Section 21 notices.

findings.detail: The Council faces a projected revenue budget deficit rising from £2.04m in 2026/27 to £10.82m by 2030/31 if unmanaged. This is primarily driven by the expiry of three major contracts (waste, leisure, and grounds maintenance), with the waste contract alone expected to more than double from its current £4.6m annual cost. Without generating sufficient savings, useable reserves would fall from £27.39m in 2024/25 to £9.43m by 2028/29, with the General Fund falling below minimum safe levels from 2027/28.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has a credible plan to close this gap before reserves are depleted. Contract cost inflation of this scale (waste doubling) is material to debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: £10.82m deficit by 2030/31; cumulative gap £38.92m over five years; waste contract from £4.6m to projected to 'more than double'; reserves falling to £9.43m by 2028/29; General Fund below minimum safe level from 2027/28
findings.quote: The Council did not rely on reserves to balance the 2024/25 or 2025/26 budgets and holds £4m in unallocated reserves, with no external debt. However, it forecasts a funding deficit of £2.04m in 2026/27, rising to £10.82m by 2030/31 if unmanaged, resulting in a cumulative gap of £38.92m over five years. This is driven by rising costs of delivering services, including the expiry of three major contracts: waste, leisure, and grounds maintenance. The new contracts are expected to be significantly more expensive due to a different economic climate. For example, the new waste and street cleansing contract is projected to more than double the current annual cost of £4.6m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A TWBC AFR 24-25 Final post completion of audit
findings.headline: Related party disclosure process had gaps; management initially failed to capture all relationships identified through independent checks
findings.detail: During audit, Grant Thornton found that some members had not submitted declaration forms or registers of interest, and some relationships disclosed were not reflected in the financial statements. Additional related party relationships were identified through independent Companies House checks that management had missed. These were corrected during the audit.
findings.matters: Completeness of related party disclosures is an audit responsibility and governance quality indicator. Gaps suggest process weakness in how the council captures and reviews related party information, with external checks needed to fill gaps.
findings.figures: Multiple members with incomplete or unavailable documentation
findings.quote: We noted that for a small number of members, either the declaration forms and registers of interest were not available for review, or the submitted documents did not capture all relevant related party relationships identified through our independent checks.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A TWBC AFR 24-25 Final post completion of audit
findings.headline: Council chose not to correct £712k pension liability overstatement identified by auditors, deeming it immaterial
findings.detail: The Kent Pension Fund audit identified £8.4m in benefits paid errors, with £142k relating to Tunbridge Wells, plus £570k in net asset valuation differences. Total impact was a £712k overstatement of the council's net pension liability. The council determined this was immaterial and chose not to adjust the financial statements, relying on unaudited KPF data that contained known errors.
findings.matters: This indicates the council's materiality judgement and reliance on third-party pension fund data with identified errors. A lender needs confidence in how councils handle misstatements and their tolerance for unaudited external data in their accounts.
findings.figures: £712k total impact; net pension liability moved from £1.568m to £0.540m
findings.quote: The total impact of these adjustments is a £712k reduction in the Council's pension liability. KPF is managed by Kent County Council (KCC) on behalf of the Council, and the audit timetable for both entities coincides. Consequently, the amounts reported in the Council's financial statements are based on unaudited information provided by KPF. The Council has determined that this adjustment is immaterial and has therefore chosen not to amend the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A TWBC AFR 24-25 Final post completion of audit
findings.headline: Journal approval controls lack preventative safeguards, with high materiality threshold for review
findings.detail: Journal entries exceeding £25,000 are reviewed retrospectively by the Head of Finance on a quarterly basis via email, after they have been posted. Entries below £25,000 have no formal approval process. The auditors noted this is weaker than best practice (requiring pre-posting approval and lower thresholds), though management defended it based on alternative controls like year-end reconciliations and supplier invoice approval.
findings.matters: A lender assesses financial control environments and fraud risk; detective controls after posting are weaker than preventative ones. This is particularly relevant given the ISA (UK) 240 presumption of management override risk.
findings.figures: £25,000 threshold; entries below this have no formal approval
findings.quote: Based on our understanding of the relevant controls around journals, we noted that journal entries exceeding £25,000 are reviewed and approved by the Head of Finance retrospectively after they have been posted. This process is carried out outside the financial system via email on quarterly basis, as the current system does not support built-in approval functionality. For entries below £25,000, there is no formal approval process in place.

findings.headline: RVP Shopping Centre redevelopment requires decisions on design and budget with council exposed as freehold and long leasehold owner
findings.detail: The council is progressing a mixed-use redevelopment of the RVP Shopping Centre but key decisions on both the recommended design and the budget to deliver the scheme are still required. The council is undertaking car park refurbishment and has appointed specialist teams, but the capital commitment remains uncertain.
findings.matters: As owner of significant freehold and long leasehold interests, the council has material capital exposure; budget decisions are pending and could represent substantial borrowing or use of reserves.
findings.figures: Current risk score 8, mitigated to 6
findings.quote: Decision required on progression of recommended designs for mixed use development scheme. Decision required on budget and build the designed scheme.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation transition must be managed while continuing to deliver existing services, with details still to be agreed by all councils
findings.detail: The government timetable requires implementation of a new unitary structure in Kent by 2028. The council is managing a significant change programme but details remain uncertain, and the council is keeping capacity and finances under review with an LGR Reserve established.
findings.matters: A major structural reorganisation creates execution risk, potential service disruption, and unusual staffing and IT costs; the establishment of an LGR Reserve signals capital resource concerns.
findings.figures: Current risk score 25, mitigated to 16; LGR Reserve established
findings.quote: The Government's timetable for implementation of LGR is within the current parliament (by 2028). This will require setting up a new unitary structure in Kent and the details of this are still to be agreed by all Councils. In doing so, transition to a new unitary structure will require implementation of a significant change programme by the Council and a need to balance this with continuing to deliver day to day services in the existing two tier structure.

findings.headline: Worsening economic conditions are reducing town centre footfall, consumer spending, and council income opportunities
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies increasing business closures in the town centre, reduced opportunities to generate income, and rising social issues including homelessness and crime as emerging pressures that the council's strategy must address.
findings.matters: Reduced commercial income and increased demand for support services creates financial pressure; a distressed high street indicates declining business rates and parking revenue.
findings.figures: Current risk score 16, mitigated to 12
findings.quote: The impact of the worsening economic conditions includes reductions in footfall in the town centre, lower expenditure by consumers, increasing business closures, reduced opportunities to generate income and increasing social issues including homelessness and crime.

findings.headline: Government funding methodology change may disadvantage the council on both population and deprivation measures
findings.detail: A new funding review will use population size and deprivation as metrics. Tunbridge Wells has grown more slowly than other Kent authorities and is the least deprived local authority in Kent, suggesting reduced relative funding under the new formula.
findings.matters: Reduced government core funding reduces revenue flexibility and may force difficult choices on service delivery or borrowing.
findings.figures: Current risk score 16, mitigated to 9
findings.quote: The Government's funding review will use a new methodology based on population size (the borough's population has grown more slowly than other Kent local authorities) and deprivation levels (Tunbridge Wells is the least deprived local authority in Kent).

findings.headline: Interest rate decline from 4% to 3.5% by March 2027 will reduce investment income
findings.detail: The economic context shows interest rates currently at 4% with official forecasts indicating base rate cuts to 3.75% by end of Q1 2026 and 3.5% by end of March 2027. The budget shows only £7k variance for investment interest, which appears insufficient to account for the impact of this rate decline.
findings.matters: Materially lower interest rates reduce investment returns, which are often relied upon to balance budgets and fund reserves growth, potentially requiring greater reliance on other income sources
findings.figures: Interest rates: currently 4%, forecast 3.75% by March 2026, forecast 3.50% by March 2027
findings.quote: Interest rates are currently 4%. current forecast is that the next rate cut will be in the first quarter of 2026, resulting in a base rate of 3.75% by the end of March 2026. The forecast for the end of March 2027 is 3.50%.

findings.headline: £250k additional budget cost due to underfunding of Employers' National Insurance by central government
findings.detail: The MTFS identifies an extra £250k cost for 2026/27 for 'underfunding of the changes to Employers' National Insurance by the Treasury and the unusual allocation by MHCLG.' This is an unfunded national policy change passed to local government.
findings.matters: This represents an unexpected cost imposed by national government without full compensation, reducing the council's financial flexibility
findings.figures: £250k additional cost for 2026/27
findings.quote: An extra £250k due to the underfunding of the changes to Employers' National Insurance by the Treasury and the unusual allocation by MHCLG.

findings.headline: Council explicitly states that using reserves to fund capital is not sustainable
findings.detail: The budget paper contains a direct statement that 'Using reserves to fund the capital programme is not sustainable' and prescribes that funding should come from disposals, grants, s106 contributions, or business rate growth. This indicates the council has been relying on reserves and recognizes this practice cannot continue.
findings.matters: This signals that reserves are being drawn down faster than sustainable, the council's liquidity cushion is shrinking, and capital funding sources may be at risk if disposals or grants do not materialize
findings.figures: Strategic Plan Reserve established at £100k; reserves forecast assumes no use of reserves to balance revenue budget
findings.quote: Using reserves to fund the capital programme is not sustainable. Funding should come from Disposals, Grants, s106 or Business Rate Growth.

findings.headline: £5.3m waste contract cost escalation from 2027/28 with no funding strategy identified
findings.detail: The waste contract is flagged to increase by £5.3m from 2027/28 onwards. The paper notes decisions on approach and results of procurement are still uncertain. The council mentions exploring options including vehicle financing and open book accounting, but no solution is confirmed.
findings.matters: A £5.3m structural cost increase on a core service represents a major unfunded liability in the medium term and signals current waste arrangements are unsustainable
findings.figures: £5.3m waste contract increase from 2027/28; also £290k leisure contract and £200k grounds maintenance increases flagged for same period
findings.quote: External contracts from 2027/28 left unchanged as decisions on approach and results of procurement are still uncertain. For reference: Waste Contract (+£5.3m)

findings.headline: Taxbase growth halved from 2% to 1% annually due to SPD and new build delays
findings.detail: The MTFS forecast has been downgraded such that taxbase growth is now only 1% per annum instead of the 2% previously assumed. This is attributed to the Spatial Planning Document (SPD) and slower occupation of new builds.
findings.matters: Structurally lower taxbase growth reduces the council's revenue-raising capacity going forward and suggests planned development is not materializing at expected rates
findings.figures: Taxbase growth revised down from 2% to 1% pa
findings.quote: Taxbase now only increases by 1% pa rather than 2% due to SPD and new build occupations.

findings.headline: Potential £1m reduction in Government Grant due to Funding Review 2.0, with damping arrangements still unconfirmed
findings.detail: The council flags that the Government's Funding Review 2.0 could result in a £1m reduction to Government Grant. The paper lists 'Government Grant will include damping arrangements' as an opportunity to close the budget gap, indicating uncertainty about whether protective damping will be applied.
findings.matters: A £1m structural loss of grant revenue (approximately 1.3% of projected spending) would be severe if not offset, and relying on government damping to avoid it adds uncertainty to medium-term planning
findings.figures: £1m potential Government Grant reduction from Funding Review 2.0
findings.quote: Government's Funding Review 2.0, no details on damping have been announced but that TW could see a reduction in Government Grant of £1m.

findings.headline: Unresolved £598k budget gap for 2026/27 requiring closure by February Cabinet decision
findings.detail: The draft budget presents a £598k gap after all subjective variances, including a 3% council tax increase (£413k) and identified pressures. findings.matters: An unfunded gap six months from final approval signals the council may struggle to balance without reserve drawdown or further service cuts

This creates a permanent arithmetic problem: costs outpace income every year.
findings.matters: If recurrent costs structurally exceed recurrent income growth, no collection of one-off savings will close the gap; the council faces unavoidable service reductions or unsustainable borrowing

This trajectory indicates fundamental structural mismatch between growing expenditure and constrained revenue growth that requires substantial intervention.
findings.matters: Escalating structural deficits present material sustainability risk to lenders and require credible multi-year savings plans; the scale here (approaching £50m cumulative) demands urgent resolution

findings.matters: Such a large cut to digital/back-office services, if not driven by a planned restructuring, could indicate the council is cutting operational efficiency investment at a time when it is already facing funding pressure—a concerning signal for service sustainability.

findings.matters: A loss of government funding this large indicates either a policy change at national level or a weakening of the council's funding position. It is structural, not one-off, and signals ongoing pressure on the council's finances.

This represents a swing from a balanced budget position and indicates the council faces a structural funding gap that must be closed through reserve drawdown, savings, or additional income before the budget can be formally adopted.
findings.matters: UK councils must balance their budgets; presenting a draft with an unresolved deficit signals the council is scrambling to find solutions and raises questions about financial planning and whether reserves will be needed to cover the gap.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: TWBC has the lowest spending power in Kent at £285 per household, with structural underfunding and no Revenue Support Grant since 2018/19
findings.detail: The council is positioned as having 'one of the lowest spending powers in Kent at just £285 per household (£282 in 2024/25)' using the Government's own benchmarking. The council 'ceased to receive any RSG from 2018/19' and faces an ongoing risk: 'There is still a risk that this council could be penalised with negative RSG'. This represents structural underfunding relative to peers and no baseline government support.
findings.matters: Lowest spending power indicates the council receives less government funding per household than peers. Negative RSG risk would mean repaying historic grant. Combined with no RSG since 2018/19, this signals structural affordability constraints.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Business rates revaluation and first-ever baseline reset in April 2026 creates funding uncertainty; pool continuation under review
findings.detail: A business rates revaluation takes effect from April 2026 alongside the 'first ever reset of Business Rate Baselines'. The continuation of the Kent business rate pool is 'under review due to the baseline rest'. The council prudently excludes business rates growth from base budget, but there is 'inherent uncertainty over the actual share of business rate growth receivable...until the collection fund is reconciled at year end'. The council assumes £500,000 of business rate growth will fund the capital programme, but forecasts 'no material business rate growth expected for 2025/26'.
findings.matters: The baseline reset is a structural change to business rates funding that could materially alter the council's position. Pool continuation uncertainty adds further risk. With no growth forecast and capital funding dependent on £500k growth proceeds, there is misalignment between assumptions and forecast outcomes.
findings.figures: Assumed business rate growth for capital programme: £500,000; forecast growth for 2025/26: no material growth; business rates revaluation effective April 2026
findings.quote: A revaluation of business rates will take effect from April 2026, along with the first ever reset of Business Rate Baselines as part of council funding. The continuation of the Kent business rate pool is under review due to the baseline rest.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Government funding reforms and autumn budget on 26 November 2025 will determine £1m of the assumed funding reduction
findings.detail: For 2026/27, the council has assumed a £1m reduction in government grant due to 'change in government methodology to distribute funding to local authorities'. The Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement is expected in December 2025. Additionally, the Chancellor's Budget on 26 November will be accompanied by economic forecasts that will determine the 'implications for Local Government and the Council' which 'will not been known until then'. This creates material uncertainty over a significant portion of the assumed budget.
findings.matters: A £1m funding assumption represents material budget risk if the settlement differs. Councils cannot reliably plan beyond November when core funding decisions are made by central government.
findings.figures: Assumed reduction £1m for 2026/27; Autumn Budget 26 November 2025; Finance Settlement expected December 2025
findings.quote: For 2026/27 an estimate reduction of £1m has been assumed from the change in government methodology to distribute funding to local authorities. Details of financial support will be set out in the Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement expected in early December 2025.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Council will commence external borrowing for the first time; reserves are largely allocated
findings.detail: The council currently has no external debt. However, the budget states: 'with reserves largely allocated it will be necessary to commence borrowing to fund additional capital schemes'. The s151 Officer will determine the appropriate mix of funding sources (capital receipts, usable reserves, or external/internal borrowing). This represents a material shift in the council's capital strategy and balance sheet.
findings.matters: Moving from zero debt to borrowing changes the council's credit profile and debt service costs. Lenders and rating agencies track this transition. The fact that reserves are 'largely allocated' suggests limited flexibility.
findings.figures: Current external debt: £0; capital application funding requirements: £2,083,930 gross project funding
findings.quote: The Council has no external debt but with reserves largely allocated it will be necessary to commence borrowing to fund additional capital schemes.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Budget deficit of £597,570 in 2026/27 escalates to £11m by 2031/32 if unmanaged
findings.detail: The draft budget shows a £597,570 shortfall for 2026/27. Without action, this deteriorates significantly: the council states the gap 'if left unmanaged increases to £11m in 2031/32'. The council acknowledges this will require 'the Council's administration to set out their prioritisation of services and allocation of the limited funding available before the final budget is set'. The consultation will ask the public to indicate their preferred allocation of funding.
findings.matters: A rapidly widening deficit trajectory signals structural affordability problems. Within five years, the gap grows more than 18-fold, indicating the council's income base is not sustainable at current service levels.

findings.quote: The Council currently has a draft budget gap of £ 597,570 which if left unmanaged increases to £11m in 2031/32.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Waste and street sweeping contract expiry will more than double the annual cost from £4.6m
findings.detail: The council's waste and street sweeping contract expires on 31 March 2027 and is expected to more than double in cost from the current £4.6m annual spend. The council describes this as 'the largest service contract this Council has ever awarded' and the significant cost increase is the primary driver of the budget gap spike to £11m in 2027/28. Separate reports on procurement will come forward as part of formal decision-making.
findings.matters: A contract doubling in cost is a material affordability issue and indicates either significant service risk or the need for substantial savings elsewhere. Lenders assess whether councils can absorb major contract cost inflation.
findings.figures: Current annual cost £4.6m; contract expires 31 March 2027; expected to more than double
findings.quote: The significant increase to the budget gap in 2027/28 is due to the expiry of the waste and street sweeping contract on 31 March 2027, which is expected to more than double in cost from its current annual cost of £4.6million.

findings.headline: Council faces abolition in April 2028 under Local Government Reorganisation with spending constraints
findings.detail: The English Devolution Bill will result in Tunbridge Wells being abolished and merged into a new unitary authority in April 2028. MHCLG has prenotified that asset transfers and spending decisions must not be detrimental to the viability of the new unitary. This constrains budget strategy to a two-year horizon with uncertainty about how deficits will be managed through or after reorganisation.
findings.matters: LGR creates strategic uncertainty and limits the council's ability to plan beyond April 2028. The prenotice constraint on spending decisions reduces flexibility to address budget deficits through asset disposal or service redesign. A successor unitary inheriting £9.9m annual deficits and depleted reserves would face acute financial difficulty.
findings.figures: TWBC abolished April 2028
findings.quote: The English Devolution Bill has been published and is working its way through the parliamentary process which will result in TWBC being abolished in April 2028. The Council received a series of letters from the Minister of State for Local Government and English Devolution which in summary, reaffirmed the timetable and set out a prenotice that asset transfers and spending decisions must not be detrimental to the viability of new unitaries.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 and abolition of New Homes Bonus will reduce government funding by £1m
findings.detail: From April 2026, the council expects to lose £1m from its baseline funding level of £2.6m as a result of Fair Funding Review implementation. This includes the loss of £852,140 in New Homes Bonus, which the government proposes to abolish without replacement. The reduction reflects the council's low population growth and low deprivation levels.
findings.matters: Government funding reductions are structural and permanent, shrinking the annual revenue base without corresponding spending reductions. Loss of NHB removes growth incentive funding, particularly disadvantageous for a district council in a low-growth area.
findings.figures: £1m reduction to baseline funding of £2.6m; £852,140 loss of New Homes Bonus
findings.quote: NHB is proposed to be abolished without any form of replacement scheme as part of the Fair Funding Review. The loss of the £852,140 NHB currently awarded forms part of the estimated £1m loss of government funding.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves fully depleted by March 2029, alongside Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves fall from £16.5m in March 2025 to £0 by March 2029. General fund reserves hold at minimum (£4.4m) only if revenue budgets are balanced, but the council's own projections show this is not achieved. The council notes this position depends on 'delivering not just a balanced budget in 2026/27 but a sustainable budget for the future', which the forecasts do not show.
findings.matters: Depletion of earmarked reserves removes the council's ability to manage budget variances or fund one-off costs. The timing coincides with LGR in April 2028, leaving the successor unitary with minimal financial buffers at the moment of greatest operational uncertainty.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves: £16,525k (Mar 2025) declining to £0 (Mar 2029)
findings.quote: The reserves and balances are currently forecast to meet the above levels although maintaining this position relies on delivering not just a balanced budget in 2026/27 but a sustainable budget for the future.

findings.headline: Three major contracts expiring 2026–2027 forecast to add £5.79m to annual costs from April 2027
findings.detail: Leisure centre management, grounds maintenance, and waste/street sweeping contracts are all due to expire between December 2026 and March 2027. The budget forecasts a £5.79m cost swing when these are reprocured. The council acknowledges bidders are seeking to limit liabilities following pandemic and cost-of-living pressures, and notes this 'presents a significant risk to the council in financial terms'.
findings.matters: Contract renewals embed permanent annual cost increases for the following 3–8 year term. A £5.79m step-change represents a material portion of the council's revenue base and is a leading driver of the £9.9m structural deficit by 2030/31.
findings.figures: £5.790 million budgetary swing for three major contracts from April 2027
findings.quote: The forecasts include a significant increase of £5.790 million budgetary swing for the cost of reprocuring the three major contracts from April 2027. Market competitiveness has returned but it is clear that bidders are seeking to limit their liabilities having experienced the uncertainties of the Covid pandemic and ensuing economic certainty and more recently the increases in the National Living Wage and Employers' National Insurance contributions. This presents a significant risk to the council in financial terms and potentially being exposed to additional risk going forwards.

findings.headline: Budget deficit forecast to grow from £1.2m to £9.9m annually by 2030/31 if unmanaged
findings.detail: The council forecasts a £1.2m deficit for 2026/27, which if left unmanaged would escalate to an annual £9.9m deficit by 2030/31. The paper explicitly states this would need to be funded from new income, further cost reductions, or central government support. The council defines a balanced budget as ongoing expenditure met from fees, charges, grant, and tax alone—but current projections show this is not being achieved.
findings.matters: A growing structural deficit indicates the council cannot balance its budget from current revenue sources and faces either significant service cuts, income increases, or unsustainable reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £1.2m deficit 2026/27; £9.9m annual deficit by 2030/31 if unmanaged
findings.quote: A budget deficit of £1.2 million is currently forecast for 2026/27, a decrease on the position reported to Cabinet in July 2025 following the approval of the Parking Charges report. If left unmanaged the deficit would increase to an annual deficit of £9.9 million by 2030/31, which would need to be funded from new income, further cost reductions or support from central Government.

findings.headline: Leisure income frozen; £290k removed from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The paper notes that "Leisure income remains frozen then £290k of income is removed from 2027/28". This suggests either a service change (closure, retendering, or subsidy model shift) or a reforecast that removes previously anticipated income.
findings.matters: A permanent removal of income (rather than growth constraint) is a structural change. It may signal changing usage patterns, service changes, or reduced commercial resilience.
findings.figures: £290k income removed from 2027/28
findings.quote: Leisure income remains frozen then £290k of income is removed from 2027/28

findings.headline: Demand pressures explicitly exceed the 3% income cap in years 3-5 of the forecast
findings.detail: From 2028/29 onwards, the budget paper cites "Demand pressures greater than income cap of 3 per cent" as the explanation for the £8m, £9m, and £9.9m deficits. This signals services are under pressure (adult social care, children's services, waste) and cannot be contained within the council's ability to raise income.
findings.matters: Demand pressures that exceed available income growth are typically non-negotiable (statutory services like social care). This signals the council will need either to reduce service scope, deploy reserves, or seek external funding.
findings.quote: Demand pressures greater than income cap of 3 per cent

findings.headline: Major contract reprocurement market costs spike in 2027/28 to £6.42m, accounting for most of that year's deficit
findings.detail: The 2027/28 deficit of £6,420k is explicitly attributed to "Market cost of reprocuring major contracts". This is a material one-time cost pressure in the third year of the forecast, driven by market pricing rather than internal spending decisions.
findings.matters: Contract reprocurement is mandatory and cannot be deferred. A spike of this magnitude (£6.4m) indicates either major contracts expiring simultaneously or significant cost inflation in the procurement market. Lenders need to know if the council has a plan to absorb or finance this.
findings.figures: 2027/28 deficit £6,420k attributed to "Market cost of reprocuring major contracts"
findings.quote: 2027/28 6,420 Market cost of reprocuring major contracts

findings.headline: Cumulative deficit of £34.5m forecast across 5 years with deficit widening each year
findings.detail: The council projects a balanced budget in 2025/26, then deficits of £1.2m, £6.4m, £8m, £9m, and £9.9m in successive years. The paper explicitly states this totals 34,526k "IF LEFT UNMANAGED", indicating that baseline spending against current income assumptions creates an accelerating shortfall rather than a plateau.
findings.matters: A cumulative deficit of this magnitude signals structural financial stress. Lenders assess whether a council's medium-term plan is credible; a £34.5m unmanaged deficit indicates the council either faces major savings/income decisions or will draw reserves significantly.
findings.quote: IF LEFT UNMANAGED [cumulative forecast totals 34,526k]

findings.detail: The MTFS notes that leisure income remains frozen initially and then £290k of income is removed from 2027/28. This represents a deterioration in the council's revenue base.
findings.matters: The loss of £290k in leisure income is permanent and contributes to the structural deficit; it signals either declining service demand or a deliberate decision to reduce income.

findings.headline: Establishment costs will increase 4% annually plus £250k to address underfunding of employers' National Insurance
findings.detail: The MTFS forecasts staffing costs growing at 4% per annum with an additional £250k per year to address backlog underfunding in employer National Insurance contributions, indicating the council previously underbudgeted for statutory employer costs.
findings.matters: An £250k annual gap in statutory National Insurance is a hidden liability now being acknowledged; 4% annual growth in staff costs exceeds typical pay awards and suggests either headcount growth or other cost pressures.
findings.figures: 4% annual increase; £250k additional cost per annum
findings.quote: Establishment costs increase by 4% each year plus £250k for underfunding of employers' National Insurance

findings.headline: Core government grants are forecast to reduce by £1m from 2026/27 due to Government Funding Reform
findings.detail: The MTFS assumes Government Funding Reform will result in a permanent reduction of £1m per annum in core government grants from 2026/27 onwards, contributing to the widening deficit gap.
findings.matters: Government funding cuts are outside the council's control and represent a structural deterioration in central support, reducing financial flexibility to manage demand pressures.

findings.quote: Government Funding Reform results in a reduction to core government grants of £1m from 2026/27

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Waste costs will increase by 6% annually plus an additional £5.3m cost from 2027/28
findings.detail: The MTFS forecasts waste as the fastest-growing cost line at 6% per annum, with a step change of £5.3m in additional costs from 2027/28. This is significantly above general inflation.
findings.matters: Waste is typically a volatile and material budget line; 6% annual growth is difficult to manage through efficiency alone and suggests either structural demand growth or market-driven cost escalation.
findings.figures: 6% annual increase; £5.3m additional cost from 2027/28
findings.quote: Waste increase by 6% each year plus £5.3m from 2027/28

findings.headline: From 2028/29 onwards, demand pressures are forecast to exceed the 3% council tax income cap
findings.detail: The MTFS explicitly identifies demand pressures as the driver of deficits from 2028/29 through 2030/31 (£7.9m, £9.0m, and £9.9m respectively), with the stated reason that these pressures exceed the constrained 3% annual council tax increase limit.
findings.matters: A structural mismatch where service demand growth outpaces income growth forces the council to choose between service reductions, further borrowing, or drawing on reserves.
findings.figures: Council tax income cap: 3% per annum; Deficits 2028/29–2030/31: £7,969k, £9,042k, £9,938k

findings.headline: Market reprocurement of major contracts will cost an additional £6.4m in 2027/28
findings.detail: The 2027/28 budget deficit includes a £6.4m line item attributed specifically to the market cost of reprocuring major contracts. This represents the largest single-year jump in the entire five-year forecast.
findings.matters: A material contract cost shock is difficult to fund from within existing budgets and signals that major services face expiring contracts or rebids at significantly higher market rates.

findings.headline: Cumulative deficits of £34.5m over five years if unmanaged, growing from £1.2m in 2026/27 to £9.9m in 2030/31
findings.detail: The council's base budget forecast projects deficits in every year from 2026/27 onwards. The deficit escalates significantly in 2027/28 (£6.4m) due to contract reprocurement, then continues to grow through 2030/31 as demand pressures outpace the 3% council tax income cap.
findings.matters: A growing structural deficit spanning multiple years represents a fundamental threat to the council's financial sustainability and borrowing capacity.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation scheduled April 2028 with constraints on asset transfers and spending decisions
findings.detail: Tunbridge Wells Borough Council is scheduled to be abolished in April 2028 under the English Devolution Bill. The Minister has directed that asset transfers and spending decisions must not be detrimental to the viability of the successor unitary authority, which constrains the council's budget discretion during the wind-down period and limits strategic flexibility.
findings.matters: LGR creates budget uncertainty and constrains strategic spending and investment decisions in the final 18 months of the council's operation, potentially limiting flexibility to address structural deficits.
findings.figures: TWBC abolition scheduled April 2028
findings.quote: The English Devolution Bill has been published and is working its way through the parliamentary process which will result in TWBC being abolished in April 2028.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Employment costs under pressure from 5% wage growth in a high-cost location with 2.5% unemployment
findings.detail: The council faces £1.072 million variance in employment costs for 2026/27. This reflects wage growth of 5% against inflation of 3.8%, compounded by operating in one of the most expensive parts of the country with very low unemployment (2.5%). Rising National Insurance contributions and the National Living Wage are driving up employer costs beyond inflation.
findings.matters: Ongoing wage and employment cost pressures erode budget flexibility and contribute to the structural deficit, with limited levers to control labour market costs.
findings.figures: £1.072 million employment cost variance; 5% annual wage growth; unemployment 2.5% (vs Kent average 3.4%); CPI inflation 3.8%
findings.quote: The rise in minimum wages and National Insurance are playing a significant part in rising employment costs.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves forecast to deplete to zero by 2029, removing budget flexibility
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves are forecast to fall from £6.663 million (March 2026) to zero by March 2029. While general reserves are maintained at the £3.0 million statutory minimum, the depletion of earmarked reserves removes the buffer for one-off spending and limits the council's ability to manage unexpected costs, savings shortfalls, or new pressures.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion indicates the council is consuming capital reserves to fund recurring expenditure, which is unsustainable and eliminates flexibility for budget variances or unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves: £6.663m (Mar-26) declining to £0 by Mar-29; general reserves sustained at minimum £3.0m
findings.quote: The reserves and balances are currently forecast to meet the above levels although maintaining this position relies on delivering not just a balanced budget in 2026/27 but a sustainable budget for the future.

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Government funding expected to reduce by £1 million from April 2026 due to Fair Funding Review 2.0
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review will implement funding changes from April 2026, reducing this council's baseline funding by an estimated £1 million (from £2.6m). This includes abolition of New Homes Bonus (£852,140) without replacement. The council states it cannot produce a reliable estimate of total funding impact due to ongoing consultations. The Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement is not expected until late November 2025.
findings.matters: Anticipated loss of £1m annual government funding removes financial flexibility and directly contributes to the growing deficit, with material uncertainty remaining until settlement is published.
findings.figures: £1 million reduction to baseline funding; £852,140 New Homes Bonus loss; settlement due late November 2025
findings.quote: The outcome of the Fair Funding Review will be implemented from April 2026, with so many changes being consulted on it is not possible to produce a reliable estimate but for modelling purposes it has been assumed that this council will see a reduction of £1m to the Baseline Funding level of £2.6m

findings.committee: Finance, Innovation and Transformation Cabinet Advisory Board
findings.headline: Three major contracts expiring 2026/27 with £5.79 million cost increase forecast for reprocurement from April 2027
findings.detail: The council faces reprocurement of leisure centre management, grounds maintenance, and waste/street sweeping contracts. Bidders are seeking to limit liabilities and pass on costs related to National Living Wage increases and National Insurance contributions. The estimated cost increase is £5.79 million, representing a material budget shock when contracts renew. Individual Cabinet reports on procurement options and mitigation strategies are still to come.
findings.matters: A £5.79m cost shock in April 2027 cannot be easily absorbed and directly threatens financial stability, yet mitigation plans are still under development.
findings.figures: £5.790 million budgetary swing; Leisure (31 Mar 2027), Grounds Maintenance (31 Dec 2026), Waste & Sweeping (31 Mar 2027)
findings.quote: The forecasts include a significant increase of £5.790 million budgetary swing for the cost of reprocuring the three major contracts from April 2027.

findings.detail: The council faces a structural deficit that would grow substantially over the medium term. Current forecast shows £1.2m deficit in 2026/27, expanding to £9.9m annual shortfall by 2030/31 if not addressed through cost reductions, new income, or government support. Bridging this would require funding from reserves or external sources.
findings.matters: A multi-year growing deficit threatens the council's financial sustainability and ability to service debt, which is a core concern for lenders assessing creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £1.2 million deficit 2026/27; £9.9 million annual deficit by 2030/31
findings.quote: If left unmanaged the deficit would increase to an annual deficit of £9.9 million by 2030/31, which would need to be funded from new income, further cost reductions or support from central Government.

news_drafts.headline: 2025/26 service expenditure delivered £1.624 million under budget
news_drafts.lead: Consistent underspends raise questions about budget accuracy and whether planned services are being delivered at anticipated levels. Combined with capital slippage, it suggests the council may not be deploying budgeted expenditure as planned.

news_drafts.headline: Investment income of £2.2 million flagged as an important source of revenue budget funding, but forecast interest rates are falling
news_drafts.lead: If investment income is essential to the revenue budget, a 0.25% rate cut reduces annual income by approximately £130,000 on the current £53.3 million portfolio. Budgets that rely on interest windfalls become unstable as policy rates fall.

news_drafts.headline: £14.074 million of capital projects rescheduled from 2025/26 into 2026/27
news_drafts.lead: Capital programme slippage indicates the council has not delivered capital projects on schedule, raising questions about procurement, planning, or execution capacity that affect the reliability of future capital delivery.
